textbookText: 3. Pulmonary respiration This type respiration takes place through the lungs on land, in which atmospheric oxygen is inhaled through nostrils. It occurs when the frog is more active and demand of oxygen is very high. Lungs are primary organs for pulmonary respiration. The route through which air enters or exits from the lungs is called respiratory tract or path which consists of nostrils, buccopharyngeal cavity, laryngotracheal chamber, bronchi and lungs.
Figure 8.4.26 Pulmonary respiratory organs a. Nostrils:

External nostrils are the paired openings situated dorsolaterally, a little above the mouth. They open into olfactory chamber of skull and then lead into buccal cavity through a pair of openings called internal nostrils. Each internal nostril is present on the either side of patches of vomerine teeth. b. Buccopharyngeal cavity: Internal nostrils open into a wide cavity which serves as a common passage of food and air called buccopharyngeal cavity. Buccopharyngeal cavity posteriorly leads in to laryngotracheal chamber through an opening called glottis. c. Laryngotracheal chamber Laryngotracheal chamber is a small thin walled chamber which performs the function of larynx and trachea. Its wall is supported by cartilages that consist of paired crescentic arytenoid cartilages and a single ring like cricoid cartilage. The inner or mucous membrane of laryngotracheal chamber is thrown into a pair of elastic horizontal folds called vocal cords. These vocal cords are stretched and relaxed by muscles connected with the cartilages. Such muscles can change the tension of cord and hence pitch of the sound too. When air from lungs is forcefully passed out between the vocal cords of laryngotracheal chamber, vibration vocal cords results the production of sound. Hence, laryngotracheal chamber is also called voice box. At the time of croaking, vocal sacs amplify the sound in male frog. Laryngotracheal chamber is connected to lungs of either side by a short tubular bronchus.
Figure 8.4.27 Laryngotracheal chamber in frog d. Lungs:

Lungs are paired, pinkish, oval, thin walled and highly elastic sacs like structures situated inside the anterior body cavity on either side of the heart. They are the chief respiratory organs and also help in buoyancy in water. They are supplied with pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins. Histologically, the wall of lung consists of three layers: outer peritoneum, middle layer of connective tissue and inner layer of epithelial cells. Peritoneum consists of simple squamous epithelium, connective tissue contains unstriated muscle fibre, blood vessels, nerves etc. and inner layer of epithelial cells. The inner surface of lung is divided into a series of small chambers called alveoli by trabeculae or septa. The inner surface of alveoli is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium having mucus secreting goblet cells. Septa are highly vascularised for gaseous exchange. There is no division of bronchi into bronchioles in lung and there are few alveoli in lungs of frog. Hence, lungs of frog are poorly developed and less efficient.

Figure 8.4.28 T.S of lung of frog Mechanism of pulmonary ventilation or breathing Pulmonary respiration takes place in between buccal respiration. Two sets of muscles i.e. sternohyal and petrohyal present in buccopharyngeal cavity have main role in pulmonary respiration. Sternohyal muscles are connected with the sternum and hyoid bone present in the lower jaw and their contraction lower floor of buccal cavity. Similarly, petrohyal muscles are Biology, Grade 11 | 418
connected with hyoid and squamosal of skull and their contraction raise the floor of buccal cavity. Process of pulmonary ventilation can be discussed under following points:

1. Inspiration: • Glottis and mouth are closed but nostrils remain open. • Sternohyal muscle contracts causing the lowering of floor of buccal cavity. • Volume of buccal cavity increases and air pressure inside the cavity decreases. • Air rushes into the buccal cavity through the nostrils from outside. • Now, mentomeckalian bone of lower jaw raises premaxillae upward to close nostrils. • Then, Contraction of petrohyal muscle takes place raising the floor of buccal cavity. • As a result, volume of bucco pharyngeal cavity decreases and air pressure in the cavity increases. • Glottis open and air rushes to lungs. (mouth and gullet are closed in this time) • When lungs are filled with air, then glottis is closed and gaseous exchange takes place in lungs for some time and buccal respiration also take place at that time.
